questions.prompt: St. Clement of Rome wrote to the Corinthian church around 96 AD, intervening in a dispute where presbyters had been deposed. Why is that letter historically significant?

questions.explanation: What makes 1 Clement notable is not its theology but its posture: Rome writes to Corinth expecting to be heeded, at a date when the apostle John may still have been alive. Whatever weight one gives that, it is early data rather than later inference.

citations.quote: The true light, which enlightens everyone, was coming into the world.

questions.prompt: St. Justin Martyr's First Apology (c. 155) describes the Sunday gathering in detail. Why does that description matter?
choices: It shows the shape of the Mass — readings, homily, intercessions, offering of bread and wine, thanksgiving, distribution — already fixed by the mid-second century
It is the first description of a Christian funeral
It proves the liturgy was originally in Latin
It shows there was no fixed order of worship
questions.correctAnswer: It shows the shape of the Mass — readings, homily, intercessions, offering of bread and wine, thanksgiving, distribution — already fixed by the mid-second century
questions.explanation: Justin is explaining Christian worship to a hostile emperor, so he has no motive to invent continuity. A Catholic reading his account recognises the structure of Sunday Mass immediately, which is a stronger argument for liturgical continuity than any later assertion.
questions.hint: He is describing it to outsiders, which is why the detail is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: True or False: Tertullian's question 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' expressed the settled view of the Fathers that philosophy has no place in theology.
questions.explanation: False. Tertullian is a Father, not the Fathers, and quoting him as though he spoke for all of them misrepresents a genuine disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask whether other Fathers agreed with him on this.

questions.prompt: Origen produced the ____, a six-column parallel edition of the Old Testament comparing the Hebrew with Greek versions — an early monument of textual scholarship.

questions.hint: The Greek prefix for 'six' gives the name.

questions.prompt: St. Vincent of Lérins offered a test for identifying authentic tradition. What was it?

questions.prompt: True or False: A person must already be a canonized saint before the Church can name them a Doctor of the Church.
questions.explanation: Sainthood is a prerequisite for the title 'Doctor of the Church,' though not sufficient by itself -- the Church additionally requires eminent learning and a formal declaration, as with Aquinas and the women Doctors.
questions.hint: The Church only calls a teacher 'Doctor' after first calling them 'Saint.'

questions.prompt: What are the three conditions for being named a Doctor of the Church?
choices: Canonised sanctity, eminent learning, and a declaration by the pope or an ecumenical council
Martyrdom, antiquity, and episcopal office
Authorship of a systematic theological work and priestly ordination
Founding a religious order and being canonised
questions.correctAnswer: Canonised sanctity, eminent learning, and a declaration by the pope or an ecumenical council
questions.explanation: Eminens doctrina is the distinguishing condition; the Church has many learned saints and thirty-odd Doctors. Note what is not required: neither ordination nor antiquity, which is why Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Ávila and Thérèse of Lisieux are among them.
questions.hint: One of the three conditions rules out most saints, and the other two rule out most scholars.

questions.prompt: True or False: The first women declared Doctors of the Church were named in 1970, more than nineteen centuries into the Church's life.
questions.explanation: True. Paul VI declared Teresa of Ávila and Catherine of Siena Doctors in 1970; Thérèse of Lisieux followed in 1997 and Hildegard of Bingen in 2012. The lateness is a real feature of the history and is better acknowledged plainly than explained away.
questions.hint: The year is within living memory for many people.

questions.prompt: St. Hildegard of Bingen, a twelfth-century Benedictine abbess, composer and writer, was named a Doctor of the Church in the year ____.
questions.explanation: Benedict XVI named her, eight and a half centuries after her death. That a medieval abbess best known for visionary writing and music should be recognised for eminent doctrine says something about how broadly the Church understands teaching.
questions.hint: It happened during Benedict XVI's pontificate.

questions.prompt: Match each Doctor of the Church to what distinguishes them.

pairs.right: The Little Way; a cloistered life of twenty-four years
A laywoman who urged the pope's return from Avignon
The Interior Castle and Carmelite reform
Visionary writing, music and natural science

questions.explanation: None of the four was ordained, none held office in the hierarchy, and one never left her convent. The category of Doctor is about the Church learning from someone, and it has never been restricted to those with authority to govern.
questions.hint: All four are women, and none of them held any office in the Church.

questions.prompt: In Augustine's mature theology (Enchiridion, ch. 30), he distinguishes 'liberum arbitrium' (free choice, which even fallen humanity retains) from 'libertas' (true freedom). What does 'libertas' specifically require that mere 'liberum arbitrium' does not?
choices: The grace that frees the will to actually love and choose the good
A formal act of the will completely independent of grace
The absence of any external constraint on decision-making
A juridical declaration of innocence before God
questions.correctAnswer: The grace that frees the will to actually love and choose the good
questions.explanation: For Augustine, fallen humanity keeps 'liberum arbitrium' -- the formal capacity to choose -- but loses 'libertas,' the actual freedom to choose and love the good rightly, which only grace restores. This distinction is the hinge of his case against Pelagius: having a will is not the same as having a healed will.
questions.hint: One of these terms describes a bare capacity; the other describes that capacity actually working rightly.

citations.quote: The preparation of man for the reception of grace is already a work of grace.
And this is true liberty, for he has pleasure in the righteous deed; and it is at the same time a holy bondage, for he is obedient to the will of God.

questions.prompt: True or False: When Augustine speaks of 'concupiscentia' in Confessions Book X, he means the same thing as an ordinary temptation that any person, fallen or not, would experience.
questions.explanation: Augustine's 'concupiscentia' names a disordered pull of desire rooted in original sin's wounding of human nature, not merely 'being tempted' -- even Christ, free of original sin, could be tempted without 'concupiscentia' in Augustine's technical sense. The term names a condition of fallen nature, not the experience of temptation as such.
questions.hint: This term describes a condition of wounded nature, not simply the experience every person has when tempted.

citations.quote: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has similarly been tested in every way, yet without sin.

citations.reference: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, Book X, ch. 30
citations.quote: disengaged from the bird-lime of concupiscence; that it may not be in rebellion against itself, and even in dreams not... commit those deformities of corruption... but that it may not even consent unto them.

questions.prompt: In Athanasius's Contra Arianos, the term 'homoousios' ('of the same substance') was chosen specifically to rule out which Arian claim about the Son?
choices: That the Son is a created being, similar to but not identical in nature with the Father
That the Son and the Father are two names for a single person
That the Son's human nature was fully absorbed into his divine nature
That the Son existed only from the moment of the Incarnation
questions.correctAnswer: That the Son is a created being, similar to but not identical in nature with the Father
questions.explanation: Arius held the Son was the highest of creatures, of a like but not identical substance to the Father. Athanasius's 'homoousios' closes that gap entirely: the Son shares the Father's very substance, not merely a resemblance to it -- the word the Council of Nicaea adopted into the Creed for exactly this reason.
questions.hint: The rejected Arian term is one letter different from the word Nicaea actually chose.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

citations.reference: Athanasius of Alexandria, Contra Arianos, Discourse I, ch. 9
citations.quote: they wrote 'from the essence of God,' in order that 'from God' might not be considered common and equal in the Son and in things originate, but that all others might be acknowledged as creatures, and the Word alone as from the Father.

questions.prompt: The Cappadocian Fathers (Basil's Letter 214, Gregory of Nazianzus's Theological Orations) fixed the distinction between 'ousia' and 'hypostasis' to resolve confusion in Trinitarian language. What does 'hypostasis' identify that 'ousia' does not?
choices: The particular person -- Father, Son, or Holy Spirit -- rather than the one shared divine nature
The physical body assumed by the Son at the Incarnation
A title used only for the Father, never the Son or Spirit
The moral character each divine Person displays toward creation
questions.correctAnswer: The particular person -- Father, Son, or Holy Spirit -- rather than the one shared divine nature
questions.explanation: The Cappadocians fixed 'ousia' as the one divine nature shared fully by Father, Son, and Spirit, and 'hypostasis' as each distinct person -- solving a real linguistic confusion, since Latin's 'substantia' and Greek's 'hypostasis' looked interchangeable but were being used by different sides to mean opposite things.
questions.hint: One term names what the three Persons share; the other names what makes each One distinct.

citations.quote: The Church uses the term 'substance'... to designate the divine being in its unity, the term 'person' or 'hypostasis' to designate the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the real distinction among them.

ousia has the same relation to hypostasis as the common has to the particular... the term ousia is common, like goodness, or Godhead; hypostasis is contemplated in the special property of Fatherhood, Sonship, or the power to sanctify.

questions.prompt: In his Homilies on Genesis, John Chrysostom uses the Greek term 'synkatabasis' to describe God's ____ -- his gracious lowering of himself to speak to human beings in ways they can actually understand.
questions.correctAnswer: condescension
questions.explanation: 'Synkatabasis' -- divine condescension -- is Chrysostom's term for how God accommodates revelation to human capacity, most visibly in how Scripture itself speaks of God in human terms so that finite minds can grasp what is otherwise beyond them.
questions.hint: This is the English word most often used to translate the Greek term, though it lacks the negative connotation the English word can carry today.

citations.quote: In order to reveal himself to men, in the condescension of his goodness God speaks to them in human words.

citations.reference: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, Homily 3, sec. 1

questions.prompt: Match each Father to the precise technical term this level introduced for their thought.

pairs.right: Libertas, distinguished from mere liberum arbitrium
Homoousios, against Arius's created Son
The ousia/hypostasis distinction
Synkatabasis, God's condescension in revelation

questions.explanation: Each of these terms did real technical work in its own controversy -- they are not interchangeable synonyms for 'grace' or 'the Trinity' in general, but precise tools forged to close a specific gap an opponent was exploiting.
questions.hint: Each term is paired with the exact problem it was coined to solve.

citations.quote: The Church uses the term 'substance'... to designate the divine being in its unity, the term 'person' or 'hypostasis' to designate the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the real distinction among them.

citations.reference: Irenaeus of Lyons, Adversus Haereses, Book V, ch. 21

questions.prompt: Augustine, against the Manichees, insists evil is privatio boni. What precise problem does this solve that his earlier Manichean view could not?
choices: It removes the need for a second, evil principle alongside God, since evil is a lack in a good thing rather than a rival substance requiring its own source
It proves evil does not really exist
It shows matter itself is evil
It explains why God directly wills particular sins
questions.correctAnswer: It removes the need for a second, evil principle alongside God, since evil is a lack in a good thing rather than a rival substance requiring its own source
questions.explanation: As a Manichee, Augustine had needed an evil principle to explain evil's existence as a rival substance. Privation dissolves the need: a lack is not a thing requiring its own cause the way a substance would, which is precisely the metaphysical move that let him leave dualism behind.
questions.hint: Ask what a dualist system needs a second principle FOR, and whether privation still needs it.

questions.prompt: True or False: In the Cappadocian settlement, 'ousia' (substance) names what is common to the three divine Persons, while 'hypostasis' names what distinguishes each.
questions.explanation: True, and getting the pairing backwards is the commonest error in this level. Before the Cappadocians the two Greek words were near-synonyms, which is part of why the earlier debates generated so much talking past each other — fixing which word answers 'what' and which answers 'who' was the actual technical achievement.
questions.hint: One word answers 'what are they', the other 'who are they' — get the assignment right.

questions.prompt: Chrysostom's 'synkatabasis' describes God's condescension in Scripture — speaking as though he has hands, or repents. What theological point does the term protect?
choices: That such language accommodates human understanding without implying God literally has a body or changes his mind
That Scripture is unreliable wherever it uses such language
That God genuinely possesses physical attributes
That these passages should be removed from the lectionary
questions.correctAnswer: That such language accommodates human understanding without implying God literally has a body or changes his mind
questions.explanation: Synkatabasis — God stooping to speak our language — lets Chrysostom hold Scripture's inerrancy and God's incorporeal, unchanging nature together. Anthropomorphic language is not an error to be corrected; it is a real accommodation doing real teaching work.
questions.hint: The term names a way of speaking down to a hearer's level without saying anything false.

citations.reference: St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

questions.prompt: Match each technical term to the Father who developed it and what it precisely protects.

pairs.right: Augustine — evil needs no rival substance to explain it
The Cappadocians — one what, three whos
Chrysostom — Scripture's accommodating language, not literal description
Athanasius — same substance, ruling out any lesser, created divinity

questions.explanation: Each term was coined or sharpened to close one specific loophole a vaguer word had left open. None of the four is decorative vocabulary; each is doing the load-bearing work of an argument.
questions.hint: Ask what imprecise word each term was introduced to replace.

questions.prompt: A friend says, 'God helps those who help themselves' -- meaning grace only kicks in after you've already done your part. Which Augustinian concept most directly corrects this?
choices: Prevenient grace, which must move the will before any good act, including the first turning toward God
Liberum arbitrium, which proves the will alone is sufficient without grace
Concupiscentia, which shows all desire is equally corrupt
Recapitulation, which describes Christ reversing Adam's disobedience
questions.correctAnswer: Prevenient grace, which must move the will before any good act, including the first turning toward God
questions.explanation: For Augustine, even the first stirring toward God -- wanting to seek him at all -- requires grace that comes before any human effort. 'Helping yourself first' gets the order backward: grace enables the willing, not merely the succeeding.
questions.hint: The Latin prefix in 'prevenient' means 'coming before' -- that's the whole point of the term.

citations.quote: The preparation of man for the reception of grace is already a work of grace.
For it is God which works in you, both to will and to do of His own good pleasure.

questions.prompt: Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Letter to Cledonius, argues 'what is not assumed is not healed.' If someone claimed Christ only appeared to have a human mind (not a real one), what would this principle say is at stake?
choices: Christ's human mind would need to be real, or else the human mind is not actually healed by the Incarnation
Nothing is at stake, since salvation only concerns the body, not the mind
The claim would strengthen Christ's divinity by removing any human limitation
The principle only applies to Christ's body, never to non-physical faculties like the mind
questions.correctAnswer: Christ's human mind would need to be real, or else the human mind is not actually healed by the Incarnation
questions.explanation: Gregory's principle, aimed originally at Apollinarius's claim that the divine Word replaced Christ's human mind, is that redemption reaches only what Christ actually took on as his own. If Christ's mind were not truly human, the human mind itself would remain outside what the Incarnation heals.
questions.hint: This is the same logic Gregory used against a fourth-century bishop who denied Christ had a full human mind.

citations.quote: Apollinarius of Laodicaea asserted that in Christ the divine Word had replaced the soul or spirit. Against this error the Church confessed that the eternal Son also assumed a rational, human soul.
If that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.

questions.prompt: True or False: John Chrysostom's homilies on wealth (including De Lazaro et Divite) argue that possessing riches is itself always a sin, regardless of how the wealthy person uses them.
questions.explanation: Chrysostom's homilies target the misuse and hoarding of wealth while ignoring the poor -- as in the parable of Lazarus and the rich man he preaches on -- not wealth's mere existence. His argument is about accountability for how riches are used, which is exactly why 'the Church shouldn't talk about money' misses his actual claim: he is not condemning possession, but indifference.
questions.hint: His target in these homilies is a specific rich man's indifference to a beggar at his gate, not wealth as such.

citations.reference: John Chrysostom, De Lazaro et Divite, Homily 2

questions.prompt: Someone tells you, 'I just need to try hard enough on my own first, and then God's grace will kick in to help me finish.' Which position from the Augustine-Pelagius controversy does this most closely echo?
choices: Semi-Pelagianism, which held that the beginning of faith could come from unaided human effort
Full Augustinianism, which this statement accurately restates
Manichaeism, which denied the goodness of the material world
Donatism, which questioned the validity of sacraments from unworthy ministers
questions.correctAnswer: Semi-Pelagianism, which held that the beginning of faith could come from unaided human effort
questions.explanation: This statement is the classic semi-Pelagian position: unaided human effort supplies the beginning of faith, with grace only assisting afterward. The Second Council of Orange (529) later condemned this exact sequencing, insisting grace must move the will even at the very first stirring toward faith.
questions.hint: This is a milder cousin of Pelagius's own position -- it doesn't deny grace outright, just moves it to the wrong place in the sequence.

citations.quote: if anyone says that this belongs to us by nature and not by a gift of grace... it is proof that he is opposed to the teaching of the Apostles.
For it is God which works in you, both to will and to do of His own good pleasure.

questions.prompt: Irenaeus argues in Adversus Haereses that Christ 'recapitulates' every stage of human life, including a real infancy, rather than appearing instantly as a grown man. Why does this matter against a claim that Christ only seemed human?
choices: Because only a real human life, lived through its actual stages, can heal and sanctify those same stages in every other human being
Because infancy is the only stage of life that matters for salvation
Because Irenaeus believed adult bodies cannot be assumed by a divine person
Because it proves Christ's mother Mary was not really human
questions.correctAnswer: Because only a real human life, lived through its actual stages, can heal and sanctify those same stages in every other human being
questions.explanation: For Irenaeus, Christ 'recapitulates' -- sums up and repeats -- the whole course of human life, undoing Adam's disobedience at each corresponding stage. If Christ only appeared human, none of those stages would actually be assumed, and the healing they accomplish for real infants, children, and adults would be nothing but appearance.
questions.hint: The logic here is the same as Gregory's 'what is not assumed is not healed,' but applied to stages of life rather than parts of the soul.

citations.reference: Irenaeus of Lyons, Adversus Haereses, Book III, ch. 18-19
citations.quote: He therefore passed through every age, becoming an infant for infants, thus sanctifying infants; a child for children, thus sanctifying those who are of this age... So likewise He was an old man for old men, that He might be a perfect Master for all.

questions.prompt: Match each objection or scenario to the Father whose argument answers it.

pairs.right: Augustine (prevenient grace)

pairs.left: Christ only appeared to have a human mind
pairs.right: Gregory of Nazianzus (what is not assumed is not healed)
John Chrysostom (homilies on wealth and the poor)

pairs.left: Christ only appeared to have a real infancy
pairs.right: Irenaeus (recapitulation)

questions.explanation: Each of these Fathers built an argument precise enough to still answer a live objection today, not just a dead fourth-century one -- the point of this level is deploying the vocabulary fixed at level 6 against something you haven't been drilled on verbatim.
questions.hint: Two of these concern Christ's full humanity; two concern grace and its practical demands.

citations.quote: Apollinarius of Laodicaea asserted that in Christ the divine Word had replaced the soul or spirit. Against this error the Church confessed that the eternal Son also assumed a rational, human soul.

citations.reference: Irenaeus of Lyons, Adversus Haereses, Book III, ch. 18

questions.prompt: Someone claims that praying to saints is unnecessary since Christ alone mediates. Irenaeus's doctrine of recapitulation offers what kind of response?
choices: It is not a direct response to this objection — recapitulation concerns Christ retracing and healing every stage of human life, not the communion of saints
It directly refutes the objection by showing saints are additional mediators
It supports the objection, since Christ alone recapitulates
It is irrelevant to any question about Christ's mediation
questions.correctAnswer: It is not a direct response to this objection — recapitulation concerns Christ retracing and healing every stage of human life, not the communion of saints
questions.explanation: This level rewards knowing what an argument is actually for. Recapitulation answers a different question (how Christ's obedience heals what Adam's disobedience broke, stage by stage of a human life) and reaching for it here would be citing the wrong Father's argument for the objection actually raised.
questions.hint: Ask what recapitulation is an argument ABOUT before deciding whether it answers this.

questions.prompt: A parish is debating whether almsgiving is optional generosity or a strict demand of justice. Which Father's argument is most directly on point?
choices: John Chrysostom, who argued in his homilies on wealth that surplus riches withheld from the poor are, in a real sense, theft from them
Augustine's Confessions, on the theft of pears
Origen's allegorical method of scriptural interpretation
Athanasius's defence of the Son's divinity
questions.correctAnswer: John Chrysostom, who argued in his homilies on wealth that surplus riches withheld from the poor are, in a real sense, theft from them
questions.explanation: Chrysostom's preaching on wealth is unusually blunt: what you possess beyond need belongs, in justice, to the one who lacks it. Matching a live pastoral question to the Father who actually addressed it, rather than to whichever Father comes to mind first, is the skill this level is testing.
questions.hint: Three of these four options are about something other than wealth and the poor.

citations.reference: St. John Chrysostom, De Lazaro et Divite

questions.prompt: True or False: Athanasius's argument that Christ must be fully divine to save us would still work if Arius had been right that the Son is a creature.
questions.explanation: False, and seeing why is the point of the level. Athanasius's whole argument is conditional on the Son actually being God: only God can bridge the gap divinisation requires. Remove that premise and the conclusion has nothing to stand on — which is why Arianism was treated as soteriologically fatal, not merely as a verbal imprecision.
questions.hint: Ask what the argument NEEDS to be true about the Son in order to work at all.

pairs.right: Augustine — grace precedes and enables the very effort

pairs.right: Gregory of Nazianzus — what is not assumed is not healed

pairs.right: Chrysostom — surplus withheld from the poor is theft

pairs.right: Athanasius — only God can bridge the gap divinisation requires

questions.hint: For each scenario, ask which Father's argument was built to answer exactly that claim.

questions.prompt: Augustine's case against Pelagius rests on attacking one specific premise. Which premise, if removed, collapses the rest of Pelagius's position?
choices: That human nature was not wounded by Adam's sin and the will remains entirely intact
That Christ's death atoned for sin
That infant baptism has any spiritual effect
That grace is entirely unnecessary for any human action
questions.correctAnswer: That human nature was not wounded by Adam's sin and the will remains entirely intact
questions.explanation: Pelagius's system depends on denying that Adam's sin wounded human nature itself -- if the will is fully intact, unaided obedience to the law becomes possible in principle. Augustine's Enchiridion attacks exactly this premise: once the will is granted to be wounded, unaided sinlessness becomes impossible, and Pelagius's entire structure follows it down.
questions.hint: This is the one claim everything else in Pelagius's system needs to be true.

citations.quote: Human nature... is wounded in the natural powers proper to it, subject to ignorance, suffering and the dominion of death, and inclined to sin.
For it was by the evil use of his free-will that man destroyed both it and himself.

questions.prompt: Match each Nestorian-style claim about Christ to the specific soteriological problem Cyril of Alexandria raises against it.

pairs.right: If she bore only a man conjoined to the Word, the Word himself was never truly born or made man

pairs.left: The divine Word and the human Jesus are two distinct subjects loosely united
pairs.right: There is no single 'I' who is both God and the one who suffered, so the cross does not actually save

pairs.left: Only the human Jesus, not the divine Word, suffered and died
pairs.right: A merely human death cannot accomplish infinite atonement for sin

questions.explanation: Cyril's recurring move is to show that Nestorius's language, whatever its intent, keeps splitting the one Christ into two subjects -- and a savior split into two subjects can no longer guarantee that God himself, not merely a man closely associated with God, is the one who died and rose.
questions.hint: Cyril's central worry in every case is the same: has the divine Word himself really become the one who suffers?

citations.quote: the holy virgin is the mother of God, not as though the nature of the Word had the origin of its being from the holy virgin

citations.reference: Cyril of Alexandria, Third Letter to Nestorius
citations.quote: If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh and was crucified in the flesh and tasted death in the flesh and became the first born of the dead... let him be anathema.

questions.prompt: Comparing Theodore of Mopsuestia's Commentary on the Minor Prophets (Antiochene) with Cyril of Alexandria's commentaries on the same texts, which best describes the difference in emphasis, without treating either as simply wrong?
choices: Antiochene exegesis emphasizes the plain historical sense of the text; Alexandrian exegesis emphasizes typological and christological meaning beneath it
Antiochene exegesis rejects the Old Testament outright; Alexandrian exegesis accepts only the New Testament
Antiochene exegesis is entirely allegorical; Alexandrian exegesis is entirely literal
The two schools produced no surviving texts that can actually be compared
questions.correctAnswer: Antiochene exegesis emphasizes the plain historical sense of the text; Alexandrian exegesis emphasizes typological and christological meaning beneath it
questions.explanation: Theodore's surviving commentary work stays close to a passage's plain historical sense, while Cyril's commentaries characteristically read the same texts for the christological pattern beneath the surface. Both are real, named, surviving approaches -- neither school is well-represented by an unsourced caricature of 'ignoring Christ' or 'ignoring history.'
questions.hint: One emphasis stays closer to what the original human author meant; the other looks for what it foreshadows.

citations.reference: Theodore of Mopsuestia, Commentary on the Minor Prophets, Preface

questions.prompt: True or False: If Arius's claim that the Son is a created being were true, Athanasius's argument that 'God became man so that man might become God' (theosis) would still work exactly as before.
questions.explanation: Athanasius's argument for theosis depends on the Son himself being fully God -- only a truly divine Son can communicate divine life to what he assumes. If the Son were merely the highest creature, as Arius held, he could not give humanity a share in a divine life he does not himself fully possess, and theosis collapses along with the premise being granted.
questions.hint: Theosis requires the one uniting himself to human nature to actually possess divine life to give.

citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

citations.reference: Athanasius of Alexandria, On the Incarnation, ch. 54
citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

questions.prompt: Augustine's City of God argues that Rome's pagan gods did not actually protect Rome from disaster, even in pagan times. Which of the following would this argument NOT directly refute?
choices: A claim that Christianity is false because it contains internal logical contradictions
A claim that abandoning Rome's traditional gods for Christianity caused the sack of Rome in 410
A claim that Rome's earlier military successes prove the pagan gods' favor
A claim that pagan worship guaranteed civic security
questions.correctAnswer: A claim that Christianity is false because it contains internal logical contradictions
questions.explanation: City of God's argument here is historical and dialectical -- it shows Rome suffered disasters long before Christianity, undercutting the specific claim that abandoning the old gods caused Rome's sack. It says nothing about internal logical contradictions in Christian doctrine, a different kind of objection Augustine addresses elsewhere, not with this argument.
questions.hint: This argument answers a claim about historical cause and effect, not a claim about logical consistency.

citations.quote: 'divine providence' the dispositions by which God guides his creation toward this perfection

citations.reference: Augustine of Hippo, City of God, Book I, ch. 1
citations.quote: For to this earthly city belong the enemies against whom I have to defend the city of God.

questions.hint: In every case here, removing one specific claim brings down everything built on top of it.

questions.prompt: Augustine's argument against Pelagius depends on establishing one claim about fallen human nature. Which, if granted, makes the rest of his case largely follow?
choices: That the will, wounded by original sin, cannot of itself turn to God without prevenient grace already at work
That human beings are entirely incapable of any good act whatsoever
That infant baptism is a merely symbolic rite
That grace is given in proportion to merit already achieved
questions.correctAnswer: That the will, wounded by original sin, cannot of itself turn to God without prevenient grace already at work
questions.explanation: Once the will's inability to initiate its own turning is granted, Pelagius's picture of unaided moral effort as sufficient collapses, and the necessity of grace at every stage — not just at the finish — follows fairly directly. Isolating the load-bearing premise is more useful than reciting the conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask which claim, if false, would make Pelagius's whole position reasonable again.

questions.prompt: Cyril of Alexandria pressed Nestorius on a specific soteriological consequence of dividing Christ into two subjects. What was it?
choices: If the man Jesus and the Word are not one subject, then it is not truly God who suffered and died, and the exchange that saves us — God taking what is ours to give us what is his — fails
That dividing Christ into two subjects makes the Trinity into four persons
That it denies Mary was a real historical person
That it makes the Eucharist impossible to celebrate validly
questions.correctAnswer: If the man Jesus and the Word are not one subject, then it is not truly God who suffered and died, and the exchange that saves us — God taking what is ours to give us what is his — fails
questions.explanation: Cyril's argument is soteriological before it is technical: unless the one who suffered is genuinely the Word made flesh, the saving exchange has no divine party to it. This is why Ephesus fought so hard over what could look like a narrow question of Christ's unity.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true of the sufferer on the Cross for that suffering to save anyone.

citations.reference: St. Cyril of Alexandria, Third Letter to Nestorius

questions.prompt: True or False: Augustine's City of God argues that Rome fell because she abandoned her old gods for Christianity.
questions.explanation: False — that was the pagan charge Augustine was answering, not his own claim. He argues the reverse: the old gods never actually protected Rome even in her pagan centuries, citing catastrophes the gods failed to prevent long before Christ. He denies the premise rather than conceding it and arguing about degrees.
questions.hint: Whose argument is being described here — the objector's, or Augustine's reply to it?

citations.reference: St. Augustine, City of God I.1

questions.prompt: Match each claim to the single premise this level shows it actually depends on.

pairs.right: That the will needs no prevenient grace to turn toward God
That the man Jesus and the Word are not strictly one subject

pairs.left: The pagan charge against Rome's fall
pairs.right: That the old gods had actually protected Rome before
That the Son is a creature rather than fully God

pairs.left: Rejecting divine images after the Incarnation
pairs.right: That God did not truly take visible, depictable flesh

questions.explanation: Every position here looks strong until its load-bearing premise is named and tested on its own. Learning to isolate that single premise is the actual skill this level is built to teach, more than memorising which Father answered which heresy.
questions.hint: For each row, ask: what ONE thing would have to be true for this claim to work?

questions.prompt: The Second Council of Orange (529) closed the semi-Pelagian controversy by canonizing which position built up across this topic's earlier levels?
choices: That even the beginning of faith requires God's prevenient grace, not unaided human initiative
That the human will contributes nothing whatsoever, even after grace is given
That baptism is unnecessary once a person has faith
That predestination guarantees salvation regardless of a person's free response
questions.correctAnswer: That even the beginning of faith requires God's prevenient grace, not unaided human initiative
questions.explanation: Orange II's canons condemn the semi-Pelagian claim that the beginning of faith can come from unaided human will, canonizing the Augustinian position built up across levels 6-8: grace must move the will even at its very first stirring toward God, while still affirming that the human will genuinely cooperates once moved.
questions.hint: This is the exact sequencing question level 7's 'try hard enough on my own first' scenario was built to test.

citations.quote: if anyone says that this belongs to us by nature and not by a gift of grace... it is proof that he is opposed to the teaching of the Apostles.

questions.prompt: Orange II condemns the semi-Pelagian formula that a person can, by natural strength alone, 'ask, seek, and knock' so that grace is given as a reward. Which earlier Augustinian argument does this condemnation draw on most directly?
choices: That prevenient grace must move the will before any good act, including the first desire to seek God
That homoousios rules out any created intermediary between God and creatures
That recapitulation requires Christ to pass through every stage of human life
That synkatabasis explains why Scripture uses anthropomorphic language
questions.correctAnswer: That prevenient grace must move the will before any good act, including the first desire to seek God
questions.explanation: The condemned formula reintroduces exactly the sequencing error Orange II rejects: treating the desire to seek God as something natural strength supplies on its own, with grace arriving only afterward as a reward. This is the same prevenient-grace argument from level 7, now shown to be precisely what Orange II made binding.
questions.hint: Look back to the level 7 question about 'trying hard enough on my own first.'

citations.quote: If anyone says that the grace of God can be conferred as a result of human prayer, but that it is not grace itself which makes us pray to God, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Eastern Fathers' language of theosis (Athanasius, the Cappadocians) and Augustine's Western vocabulary of grace describe two contradictory accounts of salvation that the Church has never reconciled.
questions.explanation: The two vocabularies emphasize different facets of the same reality rather than contradicting each other: theosis language stresses the goal (real participation in God's own life), while Augustine's grace vocabulary stresses the mechanism (how a wounded will is healed and moved). The Church has never treated these as rival doctrines needing arbitration between East and West -- they are complementary emphases from two authentic patristic traditions, not the same claim stated twice.
questions.hint: This isn't a dispute needing a winner -- it's two authentic traditions describing different facets of one reality.

citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

citations.reference: Athanasius of Alexandria, On the Incarnation, ch. 54
citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

questions.prompt: Which of the following did the Second Council of Orange (529) NOT settle, remaining a question the Fathers and later theologians continued to debate?
choices: The precise inner mechanics of how grace and human freedom interact at the moment of a free choice
Whether the beginning of faith requires prevenient grace
Whether unaided human nature can achieve its own initial turning to God
Whether grace is necessary at all for salvation
questions.correctAnswer: The precise inner mechanics of how grace and human freedom interact at the moment of a free choice
questions.explanation: Orange II definitively closed the semi-Pelagian question of whether grace must move even the will's first turning to God. It did not attempt to settle the deeper philosophical question of exactly how grace and a genuinely free human choice relate at the moment of decision -- a question later theological schools continued to debate for centuries without a single magisterial resolution.
questions.hint: Orange II answers a sequencing question, not the deeper mechanical one.

citations.quote: if anyone says that this belongs to us by nature and not by a gift of grace... it is proof that he is opposed to the teaching of the Apostles.

questions.prompt: Applying Augustine's doctrine of grace to a besetting sin someone struggles with, which prayer posture does his theology most directly support?
choices: Asking God first to give the very desire to change, not just the strength to follow through once desire is already there
Refusing to pray about it until willpower alone has produced real progress
Concluding that grace makes personal effort pointless, so no practical response is needed
Treating the struggle as proof that grace has been permanently withdrawn
questions.correctAnswer: Asking God first to give the very desire to change, not just the strength to follow through once desire is already there
questions.explanation: Augustine's famous prayer 'grant what you command, and command what you will' (Confessions X) captures exactly this: asking for grace at the root, in the very desire to change, not only for strength to execute a resolution the person has already independently formed.
questions.hint: This is the same order of operations as prevenient grace, applied to a concrete daily struggle.

citations.quote: The preparation of man for the reception of grace is already a work of grace.

citations.reference: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, Book X, ch. 29
citations.quote: Give what you command, and then command whatever you will.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what the Augustinian Synthesis level shows about it.

pairs.right: Canonized prevenient grace, settling the semi-Pelagian sequencing dispute
Complementary emphases within one reality, not rival doctrines

pairs.left: The precise mechanics of grace and free choice
pairs.right: Left genuinely open by Orange II, debated by later theological schools

pairs.left: 'Grant what you command, and command what you will'
pairs.right: Augustine's own prayer applying prevenient grace to personal struggle

questions.explanation: This level's point is distinguishing what is actually settled (the sequencing Orange II closed) from what remains a live, bounded theological question (the deeper mechanics) -- tagging the difference honestly rather than presenting every patristic claim with the same false certainty.
questions.hint: Two of these four are settled; one is explicitly still open; one is a personal application, not a doctrinal claim at all.

citations.quote: if anyone says that this belongs to us by nature and not by a gift of grace... it is proof that he is opposed to the teaching of the Apostles.

questions.prompt: Applying Orange II's teaching that even the desire to believe is itself a gift of grace, how should someone respond to a friend who says 'I want to want to believe, but I don't even have that much'?
choices: Point out that this half-desire is already a movement grace has begun, not a disqualifying deficiency to be overcome unaided first
Tell them to keep trying until the full desire arrives on its own
Explain that this shows they lack the predestined election
Advise them that nothing can be done until stronger desire appears
questions.correctAnswer: Point out that this half-desire is already a movement grace has begun, not a disqualifying deficiency to be overcome unaided first
questions.explanation: Orange II located grace at the very beginning of the process, including the first faint motion toward belief. A wish to want to believe is not evidence grace is absent; on this doctrine it is exactly what grace beginning to work looks like from the inside.
questions.hint: Ask where, on Orange II's teaching, grace is located — only at the end, or already at the start.

questions.prompt: True or False: Because theosis and Augustine's language of grace developed somewhat independently in East and West, they describe two different destinies for the redeemed.
questions.explanation: False. Different vocabularies, same reality: Peter's 'partakers of the divine nature' and Augustine's justified soul indwelt by grace are converging descriptions of one destiny, sharing in God's own life, rather than two separate outcomes. Treating vocabulary differences as doctrinal differences is a common error in reading East against West.
questions.hint: Ask whether a difference in words always means a difference in what is meant.

questions.prompt: Orange II settled that grace precedes even the first motion of faith. What did it explicitly leave unresolved?
choices: The precise inner mechanics of how grace and human freedom interact at the moment of a free choice
Whether grace is necessary at all for salvation
Whether infants require baptism
Whether God predestines anyone to hell
questions.correctAnswer: The precise inner mechanics of how grace and human freedom interact at the moment of a free choice
questions.explanation: The council answered the sequencing question — grace goes first — without resolving the harder metaphysical question of exactly how grace and a free choice coexist without either grace overriding freedom or freedom operating independently of grace. That question occupied theologians for centuries after.
questions.hint: The council fixed WHO moves first, not HOW the two forces relate once both are in play.

questions.prompt: Match each element of the Augustinian synthesis to what it actually establishes.

pairs.right: Even the desire to believe is already a work of grace
Unaided human initiative in seeking God is ruled out
The precise mechanics of grace and freedom together
Converging vocabularies for one shared destiny

questions.explanation: This level's whole point is precision about what a settled question actually settled, and what it deliberately did not. Overclaiming Orange II's scope is as much a mistake as denying its authority.
questions.hint: Two of these rows describe what WAS settled; one describes what was NOT.
